question: The support team wants to know how many orders come from customers with no city on file. Keep one row per `order_id` and one row per `customer_id`. Return the count as a whole number.
hint: Left-join orders to customers on customer_id, then count the rows where the city is missing.
solutionCode:
orders = load("ecommerce", "orders").drop_duplicates(subset="order_id")
cust = load("ecommerce", "customers").drop_duplicates(subset="customer_id")[["customer_id", "city"]]
m = orders.merge(cust, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
result = int(m["city"].isna().sum())
explanation: A left merge keeps every order, even when no customer matches. validate="m:1" checks that customer_id is unique on the right, so a repeated customer cannot double the orders. The missing city count includes orders with no matching customer, which is what the support team needs.
commonMistake: Dropping the repeated customer rows step. A repeated customer_id on the right side repeats each of that customer's orders, so the count is too high.

question: HR wants the number of employees in each department, by department name. Keep one row per `employee_id`. Join to the departments table to get the names. Return `department_name` and `headcount`, highest headcount first, then department name A to Z.
hint: Merge employees with departments on department_id, then count with groupby.
solutionCode:
emp = load("hr", "employees").drop_duplicates(subset="employee_id")[["employee_id", "department_id"]]
dept = load("hr", "departments")[["department_id", "department_name"]]
m = emp.merge(dept, on="department_id", how="inner", validate="m:1")
result = (
    m.groupby("department_name").size().rename("headcount").reset_index()
    .sort_values(["headcount", "department_name"], ascending=[False, True])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
explanation: The merge adds the department name to each employee row. Then groupby counts the employees in each name. validate="m:1" makes sure the departments table has one row per department_id, so no employee is copied.
commonMistake: Counting before the merge and then looking up names. This is fine, but merging a departments table with a repeated id first doubles every head count.

question: Growth team wants to know how many registered users have never made a transaction as the sender. Keep one row per `user_id` from the users file. Use an anti-join. Return the count as a whole number.
hint: Left-join users to the transaction user ids with indicator=True. Rows marked left_only have no match.
solutionCode:
users = load("fintech", "users").drop_duplicates(subset="user_id")[["user_id"]]
senders = load("fintech", "transactions")[["user_id"]].drop_duplicates()
m = users.merge(senders, on="user_id", how="left", indicator=True)
result = int((m["_merge"] == "left_only").sum())
explanation: indicator=True adds a _merge column that says whether each row came from the left table only, the right table only, or both. Rows that are left_only are users with no match, which is the anti-join. The sender list is made unique first, so the result is the same as a set difference.
commonMistake: Using an inner join. It drops the unmatched users, so you count the active users instead of the inactive ones.

question: Finance wants revenue by product category. Use `line_total` from the order items. Ignore order items where `unit_price` is more than 10 times the product MRP (these are entry errors). Clean the category names with stray spaces and capitals. Return `category` and `revenue` (sum, 2 decimals), highest revenue first, then category A to Z.
hint: Merge order items with products to get the category and MRP. Filter the rows. Then group and sum.
solutionCode:
items = load("ecommerce", "order_items")
prods = load("ecommerce", "products").drop_duplicates(subset="product_id").copy()
prods["category"] = prods["category"].str.strip().str.title()
m = items.merge(prods[["product_id", "category", "mrp"]], on="product_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
m = m[m["unit_price"] <= 10 * m["mrp"]]
rev = m.groupby("category", as_index=False)["line_total"].sum()
rev["revenue"] = rev["line_total"].round(2)
result = (
    rev[["category", "revenue"]]
    .sort_values(["revenue", "category"], ascending=[False, True])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
explanation: The category lives in the products table, so we merge to get it. A left merge keeps every item, and validate="m:1" checks that each product appears once. The price check compares each item with the product's MRP, so a 100x entry error is dropped without a fixed rupee cap.
commonMistake: Filtering on unit_price alone, with a fixed cap such as 50,000. Some real electronics items cost more than that, so good rows are lost.

question: The performance marketing team wants the click-to-conversion rate for each campaign. Keep one row per `click_id`. A click converts if it has a row in the conversions table. Return `campaign_name` and `conv_rate_pct` (2 decimals) for the top 5 campaigns, highest rate first, then campaign name A to Z.
hint: Left-merge clicks to conversions on click_id. Mark each click as converted or not, then merge the campaign names and take the mean.
solutionCode:
clicks = load("marketing", "clicks").drop_duplicates(subset="click_id")[["click_id", "campaign_id"]]
conv = load("marketing", "conversions")[["click_id"]].drop_duplicates().assign(has_conversion=1)
camp = load("marketing", "campaigns")[["campaign_id", "campaign_name"]]
m = clicks.merge(conv, on="click_id", how="left", validate="1:1")
m["converted"] = m["has_conversion"].notna()
m = m.merge(camp, on="campaign_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
rates = m.groupby("campaign_name", as_index=False)["converted"].mean()
rates["conv_rate_pct"] = (rates["converted"] * 100).round(2)
result = (
    rates[["campaign_name", "conv_rate_pct"]]
    .sort_values(["conv_rate_pct", "campaign_name"], ascending=[False, True])
    .head(5)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
explanation: A left merge keeps clicks with no conversion. The missing values in has_conversion become False, and the mean of that column is the conversion rate. An inner merge would drop every unconverted click and show 100 percent for each campaign.
commonMistake: Using an inner merge with conversions. It keeps only the converted clicks, so every campaign shows a 100 percent rate.

question: Growth team wants to know which signup channels bring users who never start a subscription. Keep one row per `user_id` from the users file. Count those users by `acquisition_source`. Return `acquisition_source` and `no_subscription_users`, highest count first, then source A to Z.
hint: Use an anti-join: left-merge users to subscriptions on user_id with indicator=True, then keep the left_only rows.
solutionCode:
users = load("subscription", "users").drop_duplicates(subset="user_id")
subs = load("subscription", "subscriptions")[["user_id"]].drop_duplicates()
m = users.merge(subs, on="user_id", how="left", indicator=True)
never = m[m["_merge"] == "left_only"]
result = (
    never.groupby("acquisition_source").size().rename("no_subscription_users").reset_index()
    .sort_values(["no_subscription_users", "acquisition_source"], ascending=[False, True])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
explanation: The anti-join finds users with no subscription row. Deduplicating users first means each person is counted once, even if the signup file repeats them. Grouping the left_only rows by acquisition_source gives the answer.
commonMistake: Counting rows from the users file without dropping duplicates. The repeated users are counted twice, so the channel totals are too high.

question: Food team wants the average customer rating for each cuisine, using only restaurants with at least 30 ratings. Keep one row per `rating_id`. Count the ratings per restaurant first, keep only restaurants with 30 or more, then attach the cuisine. Return `cuisine`, `avg_rating` (overall_rating mean, 2 decimals), and `n` (number of ratings), sorted by avg_rating (highest first), then cuisine A to Z.
hint: Filter on restaurant rating counts before you merge in the cuisine. The filter is per restaurant, not per cuisine.
solutionCode:
ratings = load("food_delivery", "ratings").drop_duplicates(subset="rating_id")
per_rest = ratings.groupby("restaurant_id").size()
keep = per_rest[per_rest >= 30].index
r = ratings[ratings["restaurant_id"].isin(keep)]
rest = load("food_delivery", "restaurants").drop_duplicates(subset="restaurant_id")[["restaurant_id", "cuisine"]]
m = r.merge(rest, on="restaurant_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
out = m.groupby("cuisine").agg(avg_rating=("overall_rating", "mean"), n=("rating_id", "count")).reset_index()
out["avg_rating"] = out["avg_rating"].round(2)
result = out.sort_values(["avg_rating", "cuisine"], ascending=[False, True]).reset_index(drop=True)
explanation: The 30-rating rule applies to each restaurant, so we count ratings per restaurant first. Only then do we attach the cuisine. validate="m:1" checks that each restaurant has one row in the restaurants table, so ratings are not copied.
commonMistake: Filtering by count after grouping by cuisine. That checks 30 ratings per cuisine, not per restaurant, so a cuisine with many small restaurants is wrongly kept.

question: Payments team wants the most common failure pairs. Each pair is a bank and a failure code. Keep one row per `failed_txn_id`, and one row per `txn_id` in the transactions file. Get the bank for each failed transaction through a merge. Return the top 5 pairs as `bank`, `failure_code` and `failures` (count of failed rows), highest count first, then bank A to Z, then failure code A to Z.
hint: Clean the two tables, merge the failed rows to transactions to get the bank, then count by bank and failure_code.
solutionCode:
failed = load("fintech", "failed_transactions").drop_duplicates(subset="failed_txn_id")
txns = load("fintech", "transactions").drop_duplicates(subset="txn_id")[["txn_id", "bank"]]
m = failed.merge(txns, on="txn_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
pairs = m.groupby(["bank", "failure_code"]).size().rename("failures").reset_index()
result = (
    pairs.sort_values(["failures", "bank", "failure_code"], ascending=[False, True, True])
    .head(5)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
explanation: The failed table has one row per failure, but a single transaction can fail more than once after a retry. Merging to transactions gives the bank for each failure. Two tie-breakers keep the top 5 in the same order every time.
commonMistake: Merging transactions without dropping its repeated txn_id rows. Each failure is then copied once per repeat, and the failure counts look bigger than they are.
